overview: Model deployment is the 'last mile' of machine learning. It is the process of taking a trained model and making its predictions available to end users, applications, or other systems.
In this module, we cover the technical strategies for serving models: from simple REST APIs and Microservices to high-scale Containerization with Docker.

topics.title: Model Serving & APIs
theory: The most common way to deploy a model is as a web service. When an application needs a prediction, it sends a JSON request to an API (e.g., built with FastAPI or Flask). The server loads the model, makes a prediction, and returns the result in milliseconds.
This allows the 'Frontend' (UI) to stay lean while the 'Backend' (Server) handles the heavy mathematical computations.
visualIntuition: Think of a model as a master chef. Instead of inviting the whole city into the kitchen, you have a waiter (API) who takes orders (requests) at the table and brings out the food (predictions) once it's ready.
visualSuggestions: Sequence diagram: User -> Request -> API -> Model -> Result -> User.

topics.title: Batch vs Real-time Inference
theory: Inference is the process of using a trained model to make predictions. 'Real-time' inference happens instantly for a single user (e.g., Netflix recommendations), while 'Batch' inference processes millions of records at once (e.g., monthly credit card fraud reports).
Real-time requires low latency (speed), while Batch requires high throughput (handling volume). Choosing the right strategy depends on the user's needs.
visualIntuition: Batch inference is like a mail truck that delivers all the letters once a day. Real-time inference is like a text message that arrives the moment it is sent.
visualSuggestions: Comparison table: Real-time (Low latency) vs Batch (High throughput).
Infographic showing a 'Streaming' data flow vs a 'Daily Cron' job.

topics.title: Containerization (Docker)
theory: A model that works on your computer might fail on a server due to different library versions. 'Docker' solves this by packaging the model, its dependencies, and the server into a 'Container'.
A container is a lightweight, isolated environment that runs exactly the same way on any machine—from your laptop to the world's largest cloud servers (AWS, Azure, GCP).
visualIntuition: Imagine a shipping container. You pack your goods (your code) inside it. No matter what ship (server) it goes on, your goods remain safe and untouched inside their own standard environment.
visualSuggestions: Stack diagram: Application -> Runtime -> Operating System -> Hardware.

quiz.question: What is the advantage of using Docker for model deployment?
options: It packages the model with its exact dependencies and environment, ensuring consistent behavior everywhere
quiz.explanation: Docker containers bundle the model, code, libraries, and OS dependencies into an isolated, reproducible unit. The same container runs identically on a developer's laptop, CI/CD, and production servers.

quiz.question: When would you choose batch inference over real-time inference?
options: When predictions aren't time-sensitive (daily recommendations, weekly reports) and you want lower infrastructure cost
quiz.explanation: Batch inference processes accumulated data periodically. It's cheaper (no always-on servers), simpler, and efficient for non-urgent predictions. Real-time is needed only when decisions must be immediate.

quiz.question: Compare REST APIs vs gRPC for model serving.
options: REST is simpler and widely supported; gRPC offers better performance through binary serialization and HTTP/2
quiz.explanation: REST uses JSON/HTTP — easy to debug and universal. gRPC uses Protocol Buffers (binary, smaller) and HTTP/2 (multiplexing, streaming) — 2-10x faster for high-throughput ML serving. Choose based on performance needs.

quiz.question: What is the role of a load balancer in a deployed ML system?
options: To distribute prediction requests across multiple model server instances, ensuring availability and performance
quiz.explanation: Load balancers distribute incoming prediction requests across multiple server replicas. This prevents any single server from being overwhelmed, enables horizontal scaling, and provides failover if a server crashes.
